turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Come on in, Mr. Hale. Sorry the wait ran long.
[SEG0002] person_2 (CAREGIVER): Bridge was down to one lane. We just sat there.
[SEG0003] person_1 (DOCTOR): That's a drag. What brings you in today?
[SEG0004] person_3 (PATIENT): Nights.
[SEG0005] person_1 (DOCTOR): Nights, sure. Can you tell me a little more?
[SEG0006] person_3 (PATIENT): Bathroom.
[SEG0007] person_2 (CAREGIVER): He's up peeing, err, three or four times a night. Six months of that.
[SEG0008] person_1 (DOCTOR): And how's the stream when you go?
[SEG0009] person_3 (PATIENT): Weak. Like a kinked hose.
[SEG0010] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any dribbling once you're done?
[SEG0011] person_3 (PATIENT): Yeah. Leaky faucet.
[SEG0012] person_1 (DOCTOR): Ever see blood in the urine?
[SEG0013] person_3 (PATIENT): Never.
[SEG0014] person_1 (DOCTOR): Does it hurt when you pass urine?
[SEG0015] person_3 (PATIENT): Not that either.
[SEG0016] person_1 (DOCTOR): What about urgency, that sudden gotta-go feeling?
[SEG0017] person_3 (PATIENT): Not really.
[SEG0018] person_2 (CAREGIVER): He does drink tea at night though. Two mugs of black tea after supper, every night.
[SEG0019] person_1 (DOCTOR): I have hypertension on your chart. Still being treated for it?
[SEG0020] person_3 (PATIENT): Yeah.
[SEG0021] person_1 (DOCTOR): The nurse wrote amlodipine 5 milligrams every morning. Is that what you take?
[SEG0022] person_2 (CAREGIVER): Uh, no, that's wrong. The bottle says amlodopine ten milligrams.
[SEG0023] person_3 (PATIENT): Ten.
[SEG0024] person_1 (DOCTOR): Alright, I won't lock a dose in till I see the bottle. Any headaches with the blood pressure?
[SEG0025] person_3 (PATIENT): No.
[SEG0026] person_1 (DOCTOR): Chest pain, or a tight feeling in the chest?
[SEG0027] person_3 (PATIENT): Never.
[SEG0028] person_1 (DOCTOR): Do your ankles swell by the end of the day?
[SEG0029] person_3 (PATIENT): No... well, sometimes.
[SEG0030] person_1 (DOCTOR): Short of breath when you're walking?
[SEG0031] person_3 (PATIENT): Not really.
[SEG0032] person_1 (DOCTOR): And the feet, do they get numb?
[SEG0033] person_3 (PATIENT): Feel dead.
[SEG0034] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any drug allergies?
[SEG0035] person_3 (PATIENT): No.
[SEG0036] person_1 (DOCTOR): How about the rest of you. Stomach, appetite, bowels, all okay?
[SEG0037] person_3 (PATIENT): Fine.
[SEG0038] person_1 (DOCTOR): You started telling me about a ball game outside. Did they win?
[SEG0039] person_2 (CAREGIVER): Lost, but his granddaughter got two hits. She's eight, blue cap, I take her on Thursdays.
[SEG0040] person_1 (DOCTOR): Aw, good for her. Was the weather decent?
[SEG0041] person_2 (CAREGIVER): Umm, no, it was brutal, ninety five, and the car radio was so loud I couldn't hear myself think.
[SEG0042] person_3 (PATIENT): Loud.
[SEG0043] person_2 (CAREGIVER): Then all she wanted was mint chip ice cream. Nothing but mint chip, the whole ride home.
[SEG0044] person_1 (DOCTOR): Ha. Jackhammers outside here this morning, same problem. Okay, let me look you over.
[SEG0045] person_1 (DOCTOR): Abdomen is soft, no tenderness over the bladder. Nurse got a pressure of 152 over 88 and a pulse of 74.
[SEG0046] person_1 (DOCTOR): My working impression is benign prostate enlargement, BPH, driving the weak stream and the nighttime trips. That's provisional, not confirmed.
[SEG0047] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'll book a PSA and a urinalysis so we actually have numbers.
[SEG0048] person_2 (CAREGIVER): Can he get a pill for the stream?
[SEG0049] person_1 (DOCTOR): Yes. I'm starting tamsulosin, zero point four milligrams by mouth at bedtime. I almost said tamsolosin, but it's tamsulosin.
[SEG0050] person_1 (DOCTOR): Cut the tea after supper and stop other fluids around seven. Bring the amlodipine bottle next time. If the new pill makes you dizzy, sit down and call us.
[SEG0051] person_1 (DOCTOR): Come back in four weeks and we'll review the labs.
[SEG0052] person_3 (PATIENT): Fine.

spec.situation: Older man getting up three to four times at night, weak stream, dribbling; drinks tea in the evening; denies blood in urine; PSA and urine tests planned, tamsulosin discussed.

traps.happens: The patient denies some symptoms (said as 'no', 'not really', 'never'), has a chronic condition named earlier (for example asthma or hypertension) and later the doctor asks about another symptom of it, and one answer is a double negative or a correction ('not that either', 'no... well, sometimes').
traps.label_rule: Denials go in negative_findings with the exact thing denied, never in symptoms. NEVER write a negative about a condition the patient has said they have. A corrected answer keeps only the final version. A negative is never a symptom, and 'not painful' is the finding 'pain' absent, not a symptom called 'painless'.

traps.happens: The patient describes things in colourful or sentence-like speech ('I've overdone it', 'I can't hear myself think', 'a frog in my throat', 'my feet feel dead', 'I feel like a wet rag').
traps.label_rule: Every symptom name is a short clinical noun phrase of 1 to 5 words ('voice fatigue', 'numbness in both feet', 'tiredness'), never a full sentence, never starting with I/we/my. Pure idioms that are not symptoms ('I can't hear myself think' said about classroom noise) are NOT symptoms. The patient's own words stay in the cited turn, not in the name.

features: tangent_small_talk: a long tangent or small talk (traffic, cricket, the weather, a grandchild) that holds NO clinical content; nothing from it is extracted.
disputed_numbers: the nurse reads a value and the patient or relative disagrees or remembers another (a dose, a weight, a BP). Keep both and record an uncertainty.

bad.reason: Amlodipine current, but every-morning frequency is only charted, not confirmed; dose disputed.

omissions.text: Current amlodipine dose is not confirmed: nurse chart says amlodipine 5 mg every morning, but caregiver/patient report the bottle says 10 mg, and doctor said not to lock in the dose until seeing the bottle. The recorded medication entry incorrectly lists amlodipine as currently used without dose uncertainty and attributes it to the doctor.
